questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Who sets the mode of appointing electors
questions.learningObjective: identify who controls the mode of appointing electors
questions.stem: Article Two says the legislature of each state may direct how its electors are chosen. What does that sentence establish?

options.text: That the mode of appointing electors is set by each state and not by a national rule
That the people of each state must elect their electors, since no other mode is allowed
options.misconception: believes a state may not appoint electors otherwise

options.text: That Congress appoints the electors itself, using one uniform method for all states
options.misconception: believes Congress appoints the electors

options.text: That the number of electors is fixed nationally and is the same in every state
options.misconception: believes every state has an identical elector count

questions.explanation: Article Two leaves the manner of appointing electors to the legislature of each state, so each state supplies its electors in the mode its own law provides, which is why some states use a popular vote and others a legislative appointment, and a national law purporting to impose one uniform method on the states runs into the clause that gives them this choice. Congress does not appoint electors itself, and the number of electors is set by a later amendment rather than being identical in every state, since it follows the size of each state's congressional delegation.
questions.hint: Ask which body the sentence names, and what that body may decide.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Consent required for an agreement among states
questions.learningObjective: state the consent an interstate agreement requires
questions.stem: Several states enter an agreement under which each will appoint its electors in a manner different from the one its own law otherwise provides. What does the Constitution require before such an agreement may be made?

options.text: The approval of the President, because an agreement among states is a treaty
options.misconception: believes a state agreement is a treaty needing the President

options.text: The consent of Congress, because no agreement between two or more states may be made without it
The approval of every state, since such an agreement binds those not party to it
options.misconception: believes a compact binds non-participating states

options.text: Nothing at all, because a state may always change how it appoints its electors
options.misconception: believes states need no consent to change elector rules

questions.explanation: The Constitution provides that no agreement or compact between two or more states may be made without the consent of Congress, so an arrangement in which several states bind themselves to a common rule for appointing electors is the kind of interstate agreement the clause reaches, and the requirement attaches to the making of the agreement rather than to any single state's own appointment rule. The President has no role in approving a compact, a compact binds only the parties to it, and a state remains entirely free to set its own mode of appointment on its own, which is a different act from combining with other states.
questions.hint: Ask what the Constitution requires before states act together rather than separately.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Whether a state may bind its electors by law
questions.learningObjective: state the state of the law on an unsettled constitutional question
questions.stem: A state statute directs its electors to vote for the candidate the state prefers, and the constitutional text does not say whether that is allowed. What is the state of the law on such a statute?

options.text: Forbidden, because electors represent the people and may not be instructed by a state
options.misconception: believes binding an elector is plainly unconstitutional

options.text: Allowed, because a state may set the duties of anyone it appoints to a federal office
options.misconception: believes a state may bind electors at will

options.text: Unsettled, because the text is silent and no ruling has resolved the question either way
Allowed, because electors cast their votes apart from the body that chose them
options.misconception: believes meeting separately settles the question

questions.explanation: The constitutional text is silent on whether a state may bind its electors by law, and no definitive ruling has resolved the question, which is why efforts in several states to require electors to vote a particular way have produced conflicting results rather than a settled rule. The claim that the binding is plainly forbidden reads more into the text than it will carry, the claim that a state may do as it likes with anyone it appoints confuses a federal function with state officeholding, and where the electors cast their votes has never been what decides the issue.
questions.hint: Ask what the text actually settles, and what it leaves open.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A popular-vote winner who loses the presidency
questions.learningObjective: explain how block allocation can defeat the popular vote
questions.stem: A candidate wins the national popular vote by a small margin and loses the presidency, and every state casts all of its electors for its own winner. How can that happen?

options.text: Because the national popular vote is counted from the electors' votes rather than the ballots
options.misconception: believes the popular vote is counted by electors

options.text: Because a candidate who loses a state forfeits the electors of every other state too
options.misconception: believes losing one state forfeits all electors

options.text: Because votes cast for losing candidates are left out of the popular-vote total
options.misconception: believes votes for losing candidates are not counted

options.text: Because the states won by the narrowest margins can together outweigh the states lost narrowly

questions.explanation: When a state casts all of its electors for the statewide winner, a candidate's national total is the sum of whole states won, so an advantage of a few points in several states and a deficit of a few points in one large state are not symmetrical, and the states where the margin was narrowest can together outweigh the states where the loss was narrowest. The popular vote is counted from ballots in every state, a loss in one state costs only that state's electors, and no one's votes are left out of the tally.
questions.hint: Ask what units the electors arrive in, and how large a change flips one.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Margins and block allocation
questions.learningObjective: apply block allocation to a set of state margins
questions.stem: A candidate wins a large state by 400,000 votes and loses each of two smaller states by 6,000 votes, and all three states cast their electors as a block. What does the arithmetic show?

options.text: That a much larger popular loss can cost no more electors than a much smaller popular win
That the large state's electors are weighted by population, offsetting the popular loss
options.misconception: believes electors are allocated by population share

options.text: That the two narrow losses cancel the wide win, leaving the election exactly tied
options.misconception: believes vote margins cancel arithmetically

options.text: That a state's electors are awarded to the candidate who finishes second in it
options.misconception: believes electors go to the runner-up

questions.explanation: Block allocation means a state's electors follow its winner regardless of margin, so the wide popular loss in the large state costs exactly as many electors as either narrow loss in a small state, and the size of a popular margin matters only inside a state rather than across states. Electors are not apportioned in proportion to the margin, margins do not cancel one another, and electors always go to the state's winner rather than to the candidate who finishes second there.
questions.hint: Ask whether the margin enters the calculation at all, and if so where.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The single-member bias
questions.learningObjective: explain the partisan bias of single-member plurality districts
questions.stem: Every district elects one representative and the candidate with the most votes in that district wins. Which effect does that combination produce?

options.text: It favours whichever party is strongest in rural districts, whatever the vote share
options.misconception: believes geography rather than the rule drives the result

options.text: It favours the larger party, because votes for its losing candidates are discarded
It favours no party, because every vote cast goes to a winner in its own district
options.misconception: believes the system is neutral by construction

options.text: It favours minor parties, because a large party cannot win every district outright
options.misconception: believes the system helps parties with few votes

questions.explanation: A single-member district with a plurality rule converts votes into seats one district at a time and discards the surplus, so a large party's votes concentrate where it wins while a small party's votes scatter where it loses, and that arithmetic works systematically in favour of the party with more votes overall. Whether districts are rural or urban is a separate design choice, the rule is not neutral because the conversion of votes into seats is not symmetric, and a minor party is the party least helped by discarding surplus votes.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a vote cast for a candidate who does not win.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Plurality and majority rules compared
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a plurality rule from a majority rule
questions.stem: Two rules are proposed for choosing a district's representative: the candidate with the most votes, or the candidate with more than half. Which difference follows from choosing the first?

options.text: The result turns on turnout in a runoff rather than on the first ballot alone
options.misconception: believes a plurality rule requires a second ballot

options.text: Each candidate must file papers before the result in that district can be declared
options.misconception: believes a plurality rule depends on filings

options.text: A winner can emerge without half the vote, and no second ballot is ever required
A candidate must win a majority of households rather than of the votes cast
options.misconception: believes a plurality counts households

questions.explanation: Under a plurality rule the winner is the candidate with the largest number of votes, so a winner can emerge without an absolute majority and no further election is required, while under a majority rule a candidate who wins forty per cent under one system may be required to face a second ballot under the other. A second election is what a majority rule calls for rather than what a plurality rule requires, and neither rule turns on filings or on counting households rather than voters.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the vote the winner needs, and what happens if nobody has it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A three-way district contest
questions.learningObjective: apply a plurality rule to a split district vote
questions.stem: Three candidates split the district vote 40, 35, and 25 per cent. Under the usual rule for choosing that district's representative, what happens?

options.text: Nobody is elected, because no candidate has more than half of the vote
options.misconception: believes a plurality rule requires a majority

options.text: A second ballot is held, because 40 per cent is too low to win outright
options.misconception: believes a plurality rule triggers a runoff

options.text: The seat is filled by appointment, because three candidates is too many a field
options.misconception: believes a three-way contest leads to an appointment

options.text: The candidate with 40 per cent is elected, because only the largest share is required

questions.explanation: The usual rule for a single-member district is that the candidate with the most votes wins, so forty per cent is enough when it is the largest share and no second ballot is required, and the presence of a third candidate is precisely what makes a large share possible without an absolute majority. A majority rule would demand more than half and a second ballot, and a contested election is not filled by appointment, so the second and fourth answers describe a different set of rules.
questions.hint: Ask how many votes the leading candidate needs under that rule.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: How a boundary change moves a seat
questions.learningObjective: explain how redistricting changes seats without changing votes
questions.stem: A redrawn line moves a neighbourhood of voters from a district one party wins by 5,000 into a district that same party wins by 2,000. What has the mapmaker done?

options.text: Changed which seat is won, without changing a single vote cast anywhere in the state
Changed the total number of votes cast, because redrawing changes who is able to vote
options.misconception: believes a boundary change alters turnout

options.text: Changed the number of seats in the state, because a redraw must add one district
options.misconception: believes redrawing adds seats by itself

options.text: Required every voter in that neighbourhood to re-register under a new district
options.misconception: believes redrawing forces new registration

questions.explanation: A boundary change regroups voters into districts, and because seats are won district by district, moving a block of voters between two districts the same party carried can shift a seat while every ballot in the state is cast and counted exactly as before. Redrawing does not change who may vote, does not by itself change the number of seats, and does not require any voter to re-register, so the seat moves because the arithmetic of the districts changed and not because any vote changed.
questions.hint: Ask what a voter in the neighbourhood casts, and where the ballot is counted.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A line drawn by race and a line drawn by party
questions.learningObjective: compare review of a racial line with a partisan line
questions.stem: A mapmaker draws one district boundary so that a racial group is concentrated in a single seat, and draws another to help one political party. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Both claims get the same review, because both are challenges to a legislature's mapmaking
options.misconception: believes race and party claims are reviewed alike

options.text: A claim about the racial line is reviewed under the demanding standard, and the partisan one differs
Neither claim is reviewable, because mapmaking is left entirely to the legislatures
options.misconception: believes no map may be reviewed at all

options.text: Both claims succeed automatically, because any deliberate distortion is invalid
options.misconception: believes deliberate distortion is always unlawful

questions.explanation: A district drawn on a racial line is a classification on a suspect ground and is reviewed under the demanding standard, so the mapmaker must show an interest of the highest order and a line drawn no more narrowly than required, while a claim about a drawing that favours one political party raises a different and harder question that leaves a court considering what standard it could apply. Equal review is not given to the two, and a court does not invalidate every distortion, since the difficulty of stating a standard is part of what distinguishes the claims.
questions.hint: Ask what ground each line is drawn on, and which of them the analysis reaches.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Malapportionment before the equal-population holdings
questions.learningObjective: explain why malapportionment was not treated as a legal defect at first
questions.stem: For much of the nation's history, state legislatures apportioned seats partly by county and town rather than by population, so rural counties were heavily over-represented. How did courts treat that before the modern holdings?

options.text: As a violation of equal protection from the start of the republic onward
options.misconception: believes the requirement applied from the beginning

options.text: As a matter for the national legislature alone, under its power over representation
options.misconception: believes Congress alone set state apportionment

options.text: As a question outside judicial reach, until they held that equal population was required
As a traditional practice that long usage made immune from challenge
options.misconception: believes long practice settled the question

questions.explanation: The malapportionment that over-represented rural districts went unremarked for a long time, and courts treated the question as one they should not decide because no standard told them when a departure from a traditional rule had become too great, until they held that the equal protection guarantee requires districts of substantially equal population and that such claims are for the courts. The requirement did not apply from the beginning, the national legislature's power to apportion representation among the states is a different power, and long usage did not settle the question either way.
questions.hint: Ask what a court lacked in order to decide, and what it later supplied.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The population standard for legislative districts
questions.learningObjective: apply the equal population requirement to a stated disparity
questions.stem: A state legislature gives one district 2.1 times the population of another in the same chamber. What does the one-person-one-vote rule require?

options.text: An equal number of counties in each district, which the population test does not measure
options.misconception: believes equal counties is the standard

options.text: An equal number of registered voters, which is what the rule actually counts
options.misconception: believes the standard counts registered voters

options.text: Whatever the legislature prefers, since tradition may justify a departure that large
options.misconception: believes tradition justifies a large disparity

options.text: Substantially equal population between districts, which a disparity of this size fails

questions.explanation: The one-person-one-vote rule requires that seats in a state legislature be apportioned on the basis of population, so districts of substantially equal population are the norm and a district holding 2.1 times the population of another fails that requirement, with only limited departures tolerated for local government units of a special character. Equal counties is a separate and weaker idea, the measure is population rather than registered voters, and tradition is not a permitted ground for a departure of that size.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule counts, and whether the disparity fits the tolerance.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What preclearance required
questions.learningObjective: state what a preclearance requirement obliged a jurisdiction to do
questions.stem: Before the requirement described below was ended, a covered state or county had to obtain federal approval before changing its voting practices. What did that require the jurisdiction to do?

options.text: Submit the proposed change for review by federal officials before putting it into effect
Conduct the whole election itself under federal direction from start to finish
options.misconception: believes preclearance meant federal administration

options.text: Hold the election on a single date set nationally for every covered jurisdiction
options.misconception: believes preclearance set election dates

options.text: Register every voter in its area with federal officials before the election
options.misconception: believes preclearance reached voter registration

questions.explanation: The preclearance requirement subjected covered jurisdictions to a duty to submit proposed changes to their voting practices to federal officials for review and for their assent before the change took effect, which is what made the procedure a review of the law rather than of any individual voter. It did not place the conduct of elections in federal hands, it did not fix election dates, and it did not touch the registration of voters, whose rules are set and administered separately.
questions.hint: Ask what object was submitted for review, and what came before.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The defect in the statutory coverage formula
questions.learningObjective: state the constitutional defect in a coverage formula
questions.stem: The preclearance requirement applied only to jurisdictions listed in a statutory coverage formula, and a court held that requirement to be unconstitutional. On what ground did it fail?

options.text: The statute was a bill of attainder because it named particular states outright
options.misconception: believes naming states makes a statute a bill of attainder

options.text: The formula reached whole states without the precision Congress had to use in imposing the burden
The statute had already expired by its own terms when the case was decided
options.misconception: believes the statute lapsed by its own terms

options.text: The statute conflicted with the rule against duties on goods sent out of a state
options.misconception: believes the statute regulated interstate exports

questions.explanation: The defect lay in the coverage formula, which rested on a measure the country had later abandoned as a way of deciding who belongs to the nation and so swept in jurisdictions with no more reason to suspect voting discrimination than many that the formula left out, and a statute cannot subject states to an extraordinary burden on the strength of a formula drawn no more precisely than the Constitution requires when the burden on a state is of that order. Naming a state is not a bill of attainder, the statute had not expired, and no question of duties on goods was involved.
questions.hint: Ask which states the formula reached, and how carefully it chose them.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Language assistance under the voting-rights statute
questions.learningObjective: state the language-assistance duty the statute imposes
questions.stem: A county whose voting-age population includes a substantial share of citizens who speak a language other than English holds an election. What does the federal voting-rights statute require of it?

options.text: Bilingual ballots everywhere in the country, without regard to any local population
options.misconception: believes the duty is unconditional and national

options.text: A federal observer to conduct the count on the county's behalf
options.misconception: believes observers conduct the count

options.text: Assistance in that language, once the share of such citizens crosses the statutory threshold
That every voter use a ballot supplied by federal officials
options.misconception: believes a federal ballot is required

questions.explanation: The statute requires covered jurisdictions to provide assistance in the language of a minority group where the specified share of the voting-age population speaks that language little or no English, so a county that crosses the threshold must provide that assistance, and that duty was untouched by the end of the preclearance requirement because it is a separate provision. The obligation is neither unconditional nor nationwide, federal observers attend and report rather than run the count, and no voter is required to use a federal ballot.
questions.hint: Ask what the duty is triggered by, and what the observers do.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The census and the districts built on it
questions.learningObjective: explain the sequence that produces redistricting
questions.stem: Congressional districts are drawn from population figures produced by a census taken every ten years. What follows from that arrangement for the districts?

options.text: New districts rest on the next scheduled count, because a future count is already provided
options.misconception: believes districts are drawn from a count not yet taken

options.text: Districts are permanent once drawn, because a census does not change representation
options.misconception: believes a census cannot change representation

options.text: Districts are drawn by the census bureau, which holds the population figures
options.misconception: believes the bureau draws the districts

options.text: New districts rest on the latest completed count, so shifts in population enter on a cycle

questions.explanation: Because districts are built on population figures produced by the census, and the census is taken on a fixed cycle, the map in force always rests on the most recently completed count, which is how a shift in population between one census and the next eventually appears in the number and shape of the seats. A count that has not yet happened cannot be used, a census does change representation, and the bureau supplies figures rather than drawing the map, which the state legislatures do.
questions.hint: Ask which count is available when the map is drawn, and who draws the lines.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A question referred to the electorate
questions.learningObjective: identify a referendum and describe its significance
questions.stem: A legislature refers a proposed change to the electorate instead of enacting it. What is that device, and what does it do?

options.text: A referendum, which puts a legislative question to the voters for them to decide
An initiative, which lets the voters place a question before the legislature
options.misconception: believes a referendum originates with the voters

options.text: A recall, which withdraws a serving officeholder from the office he holds
options.misconception: believes a referendum removes an officeholder

options.text: A convention, which writes a replacement for the legislature's own standing rules
options.misconception: believes a convention is a body of the legislature

questions.explanation: A referendum is the device by which the electorate decides a question the legislature has referred upward, which is what moves the decision out of the legislature's hands while leaving the subject in its hands. An initiative runs the other way, allowing voters to put a question before the legislature in the first place, a recall removes an officeholder, and a convention writes a constitution or a set of rules rather than deciding a question referred to it.
questions.hint: Ask which way the decision travels, from the legislature or towards it.

provenance.author: bank-team-usgov
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Initiative and referendum distinguished
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an initiative from a referendum
questions.stem: A state lets voters propose a law of their own and also lets them approve or reject laws the legislature has already acted on. Which pair of devices is in use?

options.text: An initiative approves a measure, and a referendum originates a measure from nothing
options.misconception: believes the two devices do opposite work

options.text: An initiative originates a proposal, and a referendum approves or rejects what a body has acted on
An initiative removes an officeholder, and a referendum convicts one of wrongdoing
options.misconception: believes either device is a removal process

options.text: An initiative chooses party candidates, and a referendum fixes primary dates
options.misconception: believes the devices belong to party nomination

questions.explanation: The initiative is the device by which voters originate a proposal, using petitions to put a measure before the electorate, and the referendum is the device by which voters approve or reject a measure that the legislature or another body has already acted on, so the two run in opposite directions and are frequently used together in a single state. A recall removes an officeholder, and neither device concerns party nominations or the scheduling of primaries.
questions.hint: Ask which device requires a petition and which requires an earlier act.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A recall and its use
questions.learningObjective: identify a recall and the function it serves
questions.stem: A state allows voters to petition to remove a sitting officeholder before the term expires. What is that device, and what does it accomplish?

options.text: An initiative, which originates a new law on a subject the legislature left alone
options.misconception: believes a recall originates a law

options.text: A primary, which narrows a field of candidates before the general election
options.misconception: believes a recall is a nomination device

options.text: A recall, which submits an officeholder's continued service to a popular vote
An impeachment, which is carried out by the legislature rather than the voters
options.misconception: believes the voters conduct an impeachment

questions.explanation: A recall is the device that puts an officeholder's continued service to a popular vote before a term ends, and it exists so that an official can be removed by the voters instead of only at the next scheduled election. An initiative originates a measure, a primary narrows a candidate field, and an impeachment is a proceeding conducted by the legislature, so the fourth answer names a real removal tool while attributing it to the wrong body.
questions.hint: Ask who decides, and at what point in the term.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The purpose of a primary
questions.learningObjective: identify a primary and its purpose
questions.stem: A state holds an early election whose sole purpose is to choose which candidate will run in the autumn. What is that election, and what is its purpose?

options.text: A runoff, held when no candidate has a majority in the general election
options.misconception: believes a primary is a repeated general election

options.text: A convention, which selects nominees by delegate vote rather than by ballot
options.misconception: believes a primary is conducted through delegates

options.text: A caucus, a party meeting that binds its delegates before a convention
options.misconception: believes a primary is a binding party meeting

options.text: A primary, held so that voters can select the nominee who will run for the office

questions.explanation: A primary is an election held ahead of the general election for the purpose of choosing a party's nominee, and its defining feature is that voters at it are selecting the candidate who will then contest the office in the autumn. A runoff decides a contest when nobody has a majority, a convention chooses nominees by delegates rather than by voters at the polls, and a caucus is a party meeting that picks or instructs delegates rather than an election of the voters at all.
questions.hint: Ask who the voters at that election are choosing, and for what.
